problem: Existing ObjectNav agents train perception and policy on expensively annotated semantic 3D meshes of simulated houses, so they cannot adapt in-situ in the real world. Most are also not tested on real robots, and supervised training may learn simulation artifacts.
motivation: A household robot should adapt to new objects and layouts after deployment without users annotating data. The paper observes that real-world ObjectNav failures are dominated by visual perception errors (4 of 6 failures were misrecognition), so self-supervised adaptation of perception is the most valuable target.
key_idea: Use location consistency (views of the same 3D cube from different angles are positives) as a self-supervised contrastive signal to fine-tune the segmentation backbone. Then use the resulting self-labeled semantic maps to train a PONI-style navigation policy, with no labeled mesh.
insight: Supervised training on simulator annotations overfits to rendering and annotation noise. Full-Seg's mIoU barely changes with or without sim noise (52.7 vs 53.1), while Self-Seg drops from 53.1 to 44.1 with noise. Full-Seg is also the worst initialization on real data (58.8 vs 61.9 for Self-Seg). The nav policy is robust to noisy self-labels: Self-Pol matches Full-Pol, e.g. 60.0/31.2 vs 56.3/28.9 with Self-Seg. Small in-situ LocCon gains on real images (+0.9 to +2.9 mIoU) show it can be applied in real houses.
method: Location-consistency data collection: build a 3D occupancy map by frontier-based exploration, sample a point (x,y,z) on occupied voxels, and place a 50cm cube there. The agent stops at 8 angles and 0.3-1.2m distances, and ray casting keeps views that hit the cube as one location-consistent group.

LocCon contrastive training: fine-tune the ResNet backbone of a pretrained DeepLabv2 (COCO-things) with an InfoNCE loss. Minibatches hold 64 locations x 4 views x 2 augmentations = 512 images, giving 7 positives and 504 negatives per image; Adam, lr 1e-5.
Self-labeled semantic mapping: run frontier exploration with the LocCon-trained segmentation model (Self-Seg) to build semantic maps of training houses with no GT labels.

Self-Pol navigation policy: train a PONI-style network to predict area and object potential functions over frontiers of partial maps, with potentials computed from geodesic distances on the self-labeled full maps.
Modular agent: semantic mapper (5cm voxels) + policy + fast-marching planner. On the real robot, an RTAB-Map pre-map supplies pose and occupancy, and (x,y,o) goals are sent to ROS move_base.
In-situ real-world LocCon: collect 479 images at 70 locations in 4 AirBnBs with a tripod-mounted RealSense, then fine-tune the segmenter with the same loss.

setting.backbone: DeepLabv2 (ResNet backbone, LocCon fine-tuned) + PONI-style policy network (trained from scratch on self-labeled maps)
setting.training_data: LocCon images from 100 unlabeled houses (random from 25 Gibson-mini train + 720 HM3D); policy trained on self-labeled maps of 25 Gibson houses; real in-situ: 479 images from 4 AirBnBs
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + pose (sim GT pose; real robot SLAM pose)
setting.action_space: sim: discrete forward 0.25m / turn 30° / stop; real: (x,y,o) global pose goals to move_base
setting.privileged: none for the self-supervised agent (sim uses GT pose; real robot uses a pre-mapped RTAB-Map occupancy map/localization)

numbers_note: Gibson-1/2 are the two Gibson ObjectNav validation sets, not canonical benchmark names. The results table has no NE column; DTS is the distance to the success radius, mapped to DTG.
results: The fully self-supervised agent reaches 60.0 SR / 31.2 SPL on Gibson-1, near supervised SemExp and PONI (65.5 and 66.2 SR, the authors' own reimplementations). On Gibson-2 it gets 36.0 SR, beating ZSON (31.3) and ZER (11.3). In the real world it reaches 66.6% over 18 tasks, and in-situ LocCon improves real-image mIoU for all models.
limitations: Real-world evaluation is small (18 tasks, 5 validation images) and relies on a pre-mapped SLAM map for localization.
Self-supervised perception is more susceptible to bad simulation renderings, and small objects remain hard for all models.
In-situ gains are small (mIoU +0.9 to +2.9, one of six failures fixed) and the policy is not adapted in situ.
